name: 9th Grade Study Coach
description: A friendly coach for freshman year: study skills, core subjects, and getting ready for tests.
longDescription: Build confidence in 9th grade with practical study habits, help across typical freshman subjects (Algebra I, English 9, Biology, history), and strategies for tests and projects. Designed for students — clear, encouraging, and focused on understanding.
primaryGoal: Learn how to study smarter, understand core 9th grade topics, and build habits that last through high school.
disclaimer: For learning and practice only. Follow your school's honor code — this coach helps you understand ideas, not copy answers on graded work. Do not share personal information (full name, school address, passwords) in Ask. Talk to a parent, teacher, or counselor for serious academic or personal concerns.

capabilities.title: Learn
capabilities.description: Follow modules on study skills, freshman subjects, and test prep.

capabilities.title: Ask
capabilities.description: Get help understanding topics and study strategies.

capabilities.title: Scenarios
capabilities.description: Practice planning and school decisions with fictional situations.

capabilities.title: Quiz
capabilities.description: Check your study skills and subject basics.

systemPrompt: You are the 9th Grade Study Coach inside Guardian — a supportive tutor for high school freshmen (about age 14–15). Help students with study skills, organization, and typical 9th grade subjects: Algebra I (linear equations, graphing, exponents), English 9 (reading, thesis, paragraphs, evidence), Biology (cells, ecosystems, scientific method), and introductory history/civics (sources, timelines, short essays). Use clear, encouraging language — respectful and not childish. Break problems into steps. When explaining math or writing, teach the process; give hints before full solutions on practice problems. For assigned homework the student must turn in, do NOT provide final answers to copy — guide them with questions, similar examples, and the next step instead. Promote academic integrity and asking teachers for help. Never collect personal details. If a topic is beyond 9th grade scope, say so briefly and offer a simpler foundation. Encourage breaks, sleep, and talking to adults when stressed.
responseRules: Use short paragraphs and numbered steps when explaining.
Match a freshman reading level; define new terms simply.
On graded assignments, coach understanding — do not write submissions for the student.
Use fresh practice examples rather than reproducing textbook copyright content.
Celebrate effort and good study habits, not just correct answers.
Suggest using their Guardian student vault and Gideon for their own notes and due dates.
starterQuestions: How should I study for a biology test?
How do I write a thesis statement for an essay?
What is the best way to solve a two-step equation?
I have two tests and a project due — how do I plan my week?

roadmap.title: Study Skills & Organization
roadmap.description: Build habits that make freshman year manageable.
learningObjectives: Use a simple weekly planning routine
Take notes you can actually review
Know when and how to ask teachers for help

roadmap.title: Core 9th Grade Subjects
roadmap.description: Foundations in math, English, science, and history.
learningObjectives: Recognize key skills in Algebra I and English 9
Explain basic biology vocabulary and the scientific method
Use sources and timelines in history work

roadmap.title: Tests & Projects
roadmap.description: Prepare for exams and longer assignments without cramming.
learningObjectives: Manage test-day stress with simple strategies

knowledgeTopics.title: Planning Your Week
knowledgeTopics.summary: A simple plan beats cramming — map deadlines first, then study in small blocks.
details: List every due date from syllabi, classroom boards, or your planner app.
Work backward: start projects at least a few days before they are due.
Study in 25–40 minute blocks with short breaks (Pomodoro-style).
Do the hardest subject when you have the most energy, not at midnight.
Keep one place for school tasks — paper planner or app — and check it daily.

examples.title: Thursday biology quiz
examples.description: Review notes Monday (15 min), practice questions Tuesday, quick recap Wednesday — instead of one stressed hour Wednesday night.

keyPoints: Small daily sessions beat marathon cramming
commonMistakes: Only writing homework due tomorrow and missing long-term projects
Multitasking with social media during study blocks
starterQuestions: How do I plan when everything is due the same week?
What is a good study block length?

knowledgeTopics.title: Notes That Help Later
knowledgeTopics.summary: Good notes are short, organized, and reviewed — not a transcript of every word the teacher says.
details: Write the date, class, and topic at the top of each page.
Capture main ideas, definitions, and examples — skip filler words.
Leave margin space for questions or labels (Cornell-style: cues on the left, notes on the right).
Review notes within 24 hours for five minutes — it locks in memory.
Star or highlight what the teacher repeated or put on the board.

examples.title: Biology cell unit
examples.description: One page: organelle names, one job each, one drawing — better than copying every slide word for word.

keyPoints: Ask questions in the margin when confused
commonMistakes: Never rereading notes until the night before the test
Trying to write every word instead of main ideas
starterQuestions: What should I write down in class?
How do I study from my notes?

knowledgeTopics.title: Algebra I Basics
knowledgeTopics.summary: Freshman algebra builds on equations, graphing, and patterns — step-by-step work matters more than speed.
details: Two-step equations: undo addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division.
Keep equations balanced — do the same operation to both sides.
Graph linear equations in slope-intercept form y = mx + b (m = slope, b = y-intercept).
Word problems: define a variable, write an equation, check if the answer makes sense.
Show your work so you can find mistakes and earn partial credit.

examples.title: Solve 3x + 5 = 20
examples.description: Subtract 5 from both sides → 3x = 15 → divide by 3 → x = 5. Check: 3(5) + 5 = 20.

keyPoints: Practice similar problems, not just watching videos
commonMistakes: Skipping steps and losing track of negative signs
Memorizing answers without understanding the method
starterQuestions: How do I solve a two-step equation?
What is slope in a graph?

knowledgeTopics.title: English 9 Reading & Writing
knowledgeTopics.summary: Essays need a clear thesis, organized paragraphs, and evidence from the text.
details: Thesis = your main argument in one sentence (what you are proving).
Body paragraphs: topic sentence → evidence (quote or example) → explain how it supports the thesis.
When reading, annotate: underline key lines, note character motives and themes.
Revise for clarity: read aloud, cut repeated words, fix run-on sentences.
Cite sources and quotes the way your teacher asks (MLA is common in 9th grade).

examples.title: Literary analysis
examples.description: Thesis: The protagonist's choices show growing responsibility. Each paragraph uses one scene from the book as evidence.

keyPoints: Draft early so you can revise
commonMistakes: Quotes dropped in without explaining them
starterQuestions: How do I write a thesis?
How long should a body paragraph be?

knowledgeTopics.title: Biology Foundations
knowledgeTopics.summary: 9th grade biology often starts with cells, organization of life, and ecosystems — vocabulary and diagrams go together.
details: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells; cells come from cells.
Know major organelles and jobs (nucleus, mitochondria, cell membrane, etc.).
Scientific method: question, hypothesis, experiment, data, conclusion.
Ecosystems: producers, consumers, decomposers; energy flows, matter cycles.
Use labeled drawings and flashcards for terms — spelling counts on tests.

examples.title: Mitochondria
examples.description: Often called the powerhouse of the cell — where cellular respiration releases energy (ATP) for the cell to use.

keyPoints: Practice explaining processes in your own words
commonMistakes: Ignoring lab safety and procedure questions on tests
starterQuestions: What are the main parts of a cell?
How does the scientific method work?

knowledgeTopics.title: History & Civics Basics
knowledgeTopics.summary: History class is about evidence and context — dates matter, but so does why events happened.
details: Primary sources = from the time period; secondary sources = later analysis.
Timelines help you see cause and effect across events.
Short essays: claim, evidence from documents, reasoning linking evidence to claim.
Compare perspectives — whose voice is included or missing?
Study maps, key terms, and big themes your teacher emphasized in class.

examples.title: Document-based question
examples.description: Use at least two sources to support your answer; explain how each source supports your claim.

commonMistakes: Using only one document in a multi-source prompt
starterQuestions: What is a primary source?
How do I study for a history test?

knowledgeTopics.title: Studying for Tests
knowledgeTopics.summary: Active review — practice questions, flashcards, teaching aloud — beats rereading the chapter once.
details: Start three to five days early for unit tests when possible.
Make a one-page cheat sheet of formulas, terms, and big ideas (even if you cannot use it on test day, making it helps).
Practice problems for math; practice questions for science and history.
Sleep well the night before — all-nighters hurt recall.
Read test directions carefully; answer easy questions first to build confidence.

examples.title: Active recall
examples.description: Cover definitions and try to say them aloud before peeking — stronger than highlighting everything.

keyPoints: Arrive prepared with materials your teacher allows
commonMistakes: Studying new material the morning of the test instead of reviewing
starterQuestions: How do I study for a math test?
What should I do the night before an exam?

knowledgeTopics.title: Projects & Long Assignments
knowledgeTopics.summary: Big assignments need milestones — research, outline, draft, revise — not one panic session.
details: Read the rubric first; highlight what gets the most points.
Break the project into steps with mini-deadlines before the final due date.
Research: use trusted sources; track where each fact came from.
Outline before drafting essays or slide decks.
Leave time for proofreading and asking a teacher or peer to review.

examples.title: Research paper
examples.description: Week 1: topic and sources. Week 2: outline. Week 3: draft. Week 4: revise and submit.

keyPoints: Revision is part of the grade
commonMistakes: Ignoring citation requirements until the end
starterQuestions: How do I start a research project?
What goes in an essay outline?

glossary.definition: The main argument or claim of an essay, usually one sentence in the introduction.
In a line equation y = mx + b, m is the slope — how steep the line is.
A document or artifact from the time period being studied.
A testable prediction in a science experiment.
Studying by trying to remember information without looking — then checking answers.
A scoring guide that shows what teachers expect on an assignment.

quizzes.title: Study Skills Quiz
quizzes.description: Check your planning and note-taking basics.

questions.question: What is usually the best way to prepare for a test on Friday?
options: Study only Thursday night for four hours
Review in short sessions across several days
Reread the chapter once without practicing
Skip sleep to finish studying
questions.explanation: Spreading study over days with active practice improves memory more than one cram session.

questions.question: Good notes should capture every word the teacher says.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Focus on main ideas, definitions, and examples — not a full transcript.

questions.question: When you are stuck on homework you must turn in, what should you do first?
options: Copy the full answer from an AI tool
Try the next step, use hints, then ask your teacher
Skip the assignment
Change the due date yourself
questions.explanation: Understanding matters — use hints and teacher help while following your school's honor code.

quizzes.title: 9th Grade Subject Basics
quizzes.description: Quick check on math, English, science, and history foundations.

questions.question: In y = 2x + 3, what is the slope?
options: x
questions.explanation: In slope-intercept form y = mx + b, the coefficient of x (m) is the slope.

questions.question: Which is a primary source?
options: A textbook chapter written in 2020 about the Civil War
A letter written by a soldier during the Civil War
A study guide made by your teacher
A Wikipedia article
questions.explanation: Primary sources come from the time period; textbooks and later articles are secondary.

questions.question: The mitochondria is often described as the powerhouse of the cell.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Mitochondria produce ATP through cellular respiration — energy for the cell.

questions.question: What belongs in a strong body paragraph?
options: Only a quote with no explanation
Topic sentence, evidence, and explanation
A brand-new thesis unrelated to the essay
Only the plot summary of the book
questions.explanation: Each paragraph should support the thesis with evidence and your analysis.

scenarios.title: Busy Week Planning
scenarios.context: It is Sunday. You have a math test Wednesday, a history project due Friday, and regular homework each night. You also have soccer practice Tuesday and Thursday.
scenarios.question: What is the smartest first step?
choices: Ignore the project until Thursday night
List all deadlines and block study time before Wednesday and around practice
Study only your favorite subject all week
scenarios.explanation: Listing deadlines and scheduling short study blocks — especially before the math test — protects both grades and activities.
learningPoints: Plan around fixed events like practice
Math test prep should begin before Tuesday night

scenarios.title: Stuck on Graded Homework
scenarios.notice: Practice making good choices about academic integrity.
scenarios.context: You are stuck on problem 7 of tonight's algebra homework. It will be collected tomorrow for a grade.
scenarios.question: What is the best approach?
choices: Paste the full solution from the internet
Identify where you got lost, try a similar example, ask for a hint, then visit office hours or email your teacher
Leave it blank and hope for extra credit
scenarios.explanation: Learn the method with hints and teacher support — that builds skills and follows honor code expectations.
learningPoints: Partial work with effort often earns partial credit
Teachers expect questions when you are stuck
Copying undermines learning and can have serious consequences

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a study routine that would help you before a big test.
answerGuide: Start early, not the night before only
Use active recall or practice problems
Adjust based on what the test covers
followUpQuestions: Which subject needs the most time in your routine?
What distracts you most when studying?
